article_title: Evaluating Interactivity: Toward Automated Assessment of AI-Generated Explorable Explanations
citation: Xiaozao Wang, Zhewei Wang, Hongyi Wen. (2026). Evaluating Interactivity: Toward Automated Assessment of AI-Generated Explorable Explanations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31012
title: FSM-based representation of interactivity as learner-controllable states and transitions (EE-Eval)
description: The article conceptualizes interactivity as "a finite space of learner-controllable states and transitions", represented as a directed graph G = (V, E, M) where V denotes semantic interaction states, E transitions, and M task-level metadata such as pedagogical intent. Interaction logic is operationalized with a JSON-based schema capturing states, events, transitions, and components, extracted from generated HTML via a few-shot LLM strategy and validated against schema constraints. Evaluation compares extracted FSMs to semi-automatically constructed ideal FSMs using structural (node/edge counts, degree distributions, density), semantic (embedding-based comparison of state labels, actions, events, metadata), and behavioral-coherence (isomorphism score) metrics, weighted 0.4/0.4/0.2 after a constrained grid search.
requirements: Requires extracted FSMs to satisfy schema constraints including state uniqueness, transition consistency, and referential integrity
Requires a pre-defined reference (ideal) FSM encoding pedagogical intent for comparison
constraints: The article states FSMs may not fully capture highly continuous or emergent interaction patterns, potentially simplifying rich user experiences into discrete transitions
Evaluation quality depends on the accuracy of FSM extraction, which may introduce noise or bias
Ideal FSM construction involves domain assumptions that may not generalize across all topics or pedagogical contexts
target_learners: Learners using AI-generated interactive learning materials in computer science education
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of computer science concepts through interactive exploration
examples: The pipeline generated 2497 explorable explanations across 127 concepts with six AI models, extracted FSMs, and computed similarity against ideal FSMs; weights (0.4, 0.4, 0.2) yielded the strongest alignment with human ratings on a validation subset.
key_sources: Xiaozao Wang, Zhewei Wang, Hongyi Wen. (2026). Evaluating Interactivity: Toward Automated Assessment of AI-Generated Explorable Explanations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31012

article_title: The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success
citation: Fathi, Z., Zarei, P., Fong, C. J., Saha, A. K., & Sharmeen, S. (2026). The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10100-9
title: Integrated theoretical framework: FSRs support success by meeting psychological needs, providing emotional security, affirming identities, and enabling campus integration
description: The article organizes its review around psychological models (self-determination theory, relationship motivation theory, attachment theory) and higher education models (the culturally engaging campus environment framework, and Tinto's and Astin's integration theories). It argues that "satisfaction of three basic psychological needs of relatedness, autonomy, and competence is essential for triggering human motivation and psychological thriving", and that attachment theory frames faculty as "secure bases" and "safe havens". Integration theories add that FSRs contribute to both academic and social integration, which together shape persistence.
requirements: The framework applies to postsecondary settings where students perceive relational closeness with faculty, not merely frequent interaction
constraints: The article acknowledges that frequent interaction does not necessarily mean students are perceiving relational closeness
target_learning_goals: academic achievement (GPA, grades)
persistence and retention
examples: The framework guided the meta-analysis's hypotheses that care-characterized dimensions and demographic/institutional factors would moderate associations
key_sources: Fathi, Z., Zarei, P., Fong, C. J., Saha, A. K., & Sharmeen, S. (2026). The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10100-9

article_title: The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success
citation: Fathi, Z., Zarei, P., Fong, C. J., Saha, A. K., & Sharmeen, S. (2026). The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10100-9
title: Six-dimension taxonomy of faculty-student relationships extracted from over a dozen measures
description: To handle heterogeneity across FSR measures, the authors inductively reviewed more than a dozen survey instruments and derived a categorical coding scheme. As they state, "we extracted the following six dimensions: caring attitude, approachability and accessibility, personal connection and bonding, inclusivity, mutual respect, and encouragement and engagement." Each dimension has an operational definition and sample items (Table 2), and each effect size was flagged via a checklist approach for which dimensions its measure contained, enabling dimension-based moderator analysis.
requirements: Coding requires examining original scale items to determine which relational dimensions a measure captures, since not all surveys consistently contain items tapping these dimensions
constraints: The dimensions were coded qualitatively from measures, and a single scale could capture multiple dimensions, so dimension flags are not mutually exclusive
target_learning_goals: conceptualizing and measuring perceived relational closeness with faculty
examples: Table 2 lists operational definitions and sample items, e.g., caring attitude: "My professor cares about students' well-being"
key_sources: Fathi, Z., Zarei, P., Fong, C. J., Saha, A. K., & Sharmeen, S. (2026). The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10100-9

article_title: Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation
citation: Nancy C. Jordan, Nancy Dyson, Taylor-Paige Guba, Megan Botello, Heather Suchanec-Cooper, Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2024.105954
title: FSI theory of change linking intervention components, science-of-learning principles, cognitive processes, and proximal and distal outcomes
description: The article presents a theory of change model (Figure 1) grounding the FSI in numerical cognition research. It maps three intervention components (fractions as numbers with magnitudes, fraction arithmetic computation, fractions applied to real-world situations) through science-of-learning principles and underlying cognitive processes (numerical magnitude understanding, proportional and multiplicative reasoning, mathematical equivalence) to proximal outcomes such as "Improved knowledge in: Fraction concepts" and distal outcomes including better preparedness for algebra. Teacher fidelity of implementation is named a possible mediator and student characteristics possible moderators.
requirements: Implementation by teachers within their intervention classrooms, with usability and feasibility prioritized in the design
constraints: Real-world occurrences in the classroom might encourage deviation from FSI lessons, making fidelity a potential mediator
target_learning_goals: fraction concepts
fraction arithmetic and its conceptual underpinnings
fraction fluency
fraction attitudes and motivation
examples: The model's principles are instantiated in the 24 animated PowerPoint lessons, e.g., a color-run race narrative maps a number line onto the racecourse.
key_sources: Nancy C. Jordan, Nancy Dyson, Taylor-Paige Guba, Megan Botello, Heather Suchanec-Cooper, Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2024.105954

article_title: Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation
citation: Nancy C. Jordan, Nancy Dyson, Taylor-Paige Guba, Megan Botello, Heather Suchanec-Cooper, Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2024.105954
title: Five-activity lesson structure with short, predictable activities for intervention lessons
description: Each FSI lesson follows five predictable activities: Sprint (~3 min) multiplication fluency practice, Warm Up (~1-3 min) review of prior content, Huddle (~18 min) main instruction with slides and manipulatives, Game-based Practice (~5 min) retrieval-based games with whiteboards, and Cool Down (~3-5 min) interleaved independent problems serving as formative assessment. The article states "Short activities hold students' attention by providing a variety of contexts for learning targeted concepts." The Cool Down structure "allowed for distributed and interleaved practice at the conclusion of each lesson."
requirements: A workbook with color-coded pages for each activity and animated PowerPoint slides presented by the teacher
constraints: The intervention was designed for a 30-minute class, which can be difficult for teachers preparing 50-minute sessions
target_learners: sixth-grade students with mathematics difficulties in intervention classes
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude concepts
fraction arithmetic fluency
examples: Sprints presented multiplication combinations with one of three numbers missing (e.g., 4 x 3 =___; ___x 3 = 12; or 4 x ___ =12).
key_sources: Nancy C. Jordan, Nancy Dyson, Taylor-Paige Guba, Megan Botello, Heather Suchanec-Cooper, Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2024.105954

article_title: Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation
citation: Nancy C. Jordan, Nancy Dyson, Taylor-Paige Guba, Megan Botello, Heather Suchanec-Cooper, Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2024.105954
title: Embed science-of-learning principles (meaningful contexts, gestures, concreteness fading, integrated visual-verbal models, interleaved retrieval practice, process-oriented feedback) in fraction intervention design
description: The FSI explicitly employs principles grounded in research in the science of learning to maximize effectiveness and encourage retention of fraction concepts. Lessons anchor instruction in a meaningful color-run race narrative, use animated gestures with an arrow sweeping from 0 to the fraction, apply concreteness fading from physical fraction bars to drawings to mental models, place text next to visualizations to decrease memory load, use side-by-side comparisons of worked examples, spiral concepts with increasingly larger denominators for distributed and interleaved practice, and provide corrective and process-oriented feedback.
requirements: Teacher training on the learning science principles and how to present the PowerPoint lessons
constraints: The article notes these principles are drawn from prior research (e.g., Bottge et al., 2014; Fyfe & Nathan, 2019) rather than independently tested in this study
target_learning_goals: fraction sense-making rather than procedure memorization
retention and application of fraction concepts
examples: When a student compared 7/8 and 1/4 with a suboptimal strategy, the instructor showed benchmarking and explained why the choice made sense to encourage metacognition.
key_sources: Nancy C. Jordan, Nancy Dyson, Taylor-Paige Guba, Megan Botello, Heather Suchanec-Cooper, Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2024.105954

article_title: Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation
citation: Nancy C. Jordan, Nancy Dyson, Taylor-Paige Guba, Megan Botello, Heather Suchanec-Cooper, Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2024.105954
title: Fraction Sense Intervention (FSI): 24 animated PowerPoint lessons with magnetic fraction bars and racecourse number lines
description: The FSI consists of 24 animated PowerPoint (APP) lessons with scripts on the slides, situated in a story about a student planning a color-run race, with drink stations at every half mile and color throw stations at every fourth mile. Students use magnetic acrylic fraction bars and partitioned racecourse number lines on a metal pan; unlabeled bars require students to reason about fraction values relative to the whole. Preliminary work showed the approach was feasible and usable in authentic classroom settings, with teachers reporting it is easy to use and requires minimal preparation time.
requirements: A three-hour training session led by researchers before implementing the lessons
constraints: Average teacher fidelity to the script was 79%; six of 11 FSI classes received all 24 lessons, three received 22, and two received 20 or less
target_learners: sixth-grade students with mathematics difficulties in whole-class intervention settings
target_learning_goals: fractions as numbers with magnitudes
equivalent fractions
fraction arithmetic
examples: The racecourse model let students see a drink station and a color throw station at the same distance, giving meaning to equivalent fractions.
key_sources: Nancy C. Jordan, Nancy Dyson, Taylor-Paige Guba, Megan Botello, Heather Suchanec-Cooper, Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Impact of a Fraction Sense Intervention in Authentic School Environments: An Initial Investigation. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2024.105954

article_title: Efficacy Validation of the Revised First Step Program: A Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Feil, E. G., Walker, H. M., Frey, A. J., Seeley, J. R., Small, J. W., Golly, A., Lee, J., & Forness, S. R. (2020). Efficacy Validation of the Revised First Step Program: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Exceptional Children. https://journals.sagepub.com/home/ecx
title: First Step Next core component pattern: direct instruction, contingencies, peer and home support, rewards, and dense positive feedback
description: The FSN revision preserved the core elements credited with the original program's efficacy: "direct instruction in school success skills, group and individual contingencies, peer and home support, school and home reward activities, and a dense schedule of positive feedback and descriptive praise." These components operate across classroom and home settings and were retained while streamlining the program for easier implementation with integrity.
requirements: Coach and teacher delivery of the core components, monitored via fidelity checks
A focus child identified through multi-stage behavioral screening
target_learners: preschool through grade 2 children at risk for school failure due to externalizing behavior
target_learning_goals: school success skills
social-emotional skill mastery
examples: The revision added Super Student Skill Lessons teaching seven discrete skills (e.g., follow directions, be cool, be a team player) and expanded the coach phase from 5 to 7 program days

article_title: Effectiveness of the Preschool Version of the First Step to Success Early Intervention Program for Preventing Antisocial Behaviors
citation: Çelik, S., Diken, İ. H., Çolak, A., Arıkan, A., Bozkurt, F., & Tomris, G. (2016). Effectiveness of the preschool version of the first step to success early intervention program for preventing antisocial behaviors. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 511-535. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.2.0317
title: First Step to Success Preschool Version (FSS-PSV) early intervention program
description: FSS-PSV is an early intervention program for preschool children at risk of antisocial behaviors that operates across the child's home and school environments. The article describes it as having "three interrelated dynamic modules: (1) Screening module, (2) Class module, and (3) Home module," delivered through seven small booklets. In this study, counselors modeled the class module for five days using a green-red feedback card and award menu, teachers continued it for 30 school days, and parents applied home module activity cards for six weeks covering communication, collaboration, rules, problem-solving, and friendships.
requirements: Volunteer participation of parents and teachers with oral and written approvals
A trained FSS-PSV counselor to model the class module and coach families weekly
Teachers record daily progress and send the Daily Green-Red Feedback Card to parents
constraints: Implementation days varied when teachers or students were absent (20 to 30 weekdays across the six implementing teachers)
target_learners: Preschool children aged 36-72 months at risk of antisocial behaviors
target_learning_goals: Reducing externalized problem behaviors
Developing social skills such as communication, collaboration, and friendship
examples: Counselors implemented the class module for the first five days as a model; teachers implemented from day six; the home module began on day 11 and lasted six weeks with weekly parent meetings
key_sources: Çelik, S., Diken, İ. H., Çolak, A., Arıkan, A., Bozkurt, F., & Tomris, G. (2016). Effectiveness of the preschool version of the first step to success early intervention program for preventing antisocial behaviors. Effectiveness of the preschool version of the first step to success early intervention program for preventing antisocial behaviors. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 16, 511-535. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2016.2.0317
title: Implement the class and home modules of FSS-PSV connectedly, since their combination is credited as a key factor in the program's success
description: The article recommends delivering FSS-PSV's school and home components together rather than in isolation. In discussing why problem behaviors decreased, the authors state that "implementation of the class and home modules connectedly was one of the most important factor affecting the success of the program," and cite other FSS studies showing the combined modules had a deep impact on decreasing and maintaining reductions in problem behaviors.
requirements: Teachers implementing the class module and parents implementing the home module with weekly counselor support
Daily green-red feedback cards linking school performance to home rewards
constraints: The study was conducted in the first semester of the academic year, and absences disrupted the 30-weekday implementation in some schools
target_learners: Preschool children at risk of antisocial behaviors and their families and teachers
target_learning_goals: Decreasing and maintaining reductions in problem behaviors across school and home settings
examples: In this study the class module ran for 30 school days with a green-red card and award menu, while the home module ran six weeks with weekly parent meetings and daily feedback cards sent home

article_title: Teaching Formulaic Sequences in the Classroom: Effects on Spoken Fluency
citation: Michael McGuire & Jenifer Larson-Hall. (2017). Teaching Formulaic Sequences in the Classroom: Effects on Spoken Fluency. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 1–25. http://dx.doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1271
title: Five-week FS-focused task-based course with weekly topic conversations and graded production
description: A unit-level instructional pattern in which each week centers on one recorded native-speaker conversation about a conversational topic. Session one builds listening comprehension identically for all learners; session two diverges, with the treatment group mining the transcript for FS and exploring usage; session three centers on production, with students expected to use learned FS while speaking. About half of course time was given to speaking practice, and explicit grammar was not taught at all.
requirements: Voluntary class meeting 30 minutes three times weekly over five weeks
Different instructors per group following agreed-upon lesson plans
Pretest and posttest dialogic conversations on the same topic
constraints: Attrition was high: only 19 of 40 initial students completed; two sessions were cancelled due to instructor illness, so students could attend at most eight hours of class
target_learners: mid-intermediate to advanced ESL learners in an intensive university preparation program
target_learning_goals: spoken fluency in dialogic tasks
noticing and producing formulaic sequences
examples: Each week focused on a different recorded conversation, such as the Week 3 topic Living Places, with FS underlined in the transcript for the treatment group
key_sources: Michael McGuire & Jenifer Larson-Hall. (2017). Teaching Formulaic Sequences in the Classroom: Effects on Spoken Fluency. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 1–25. http://dx.doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1271

article_title: The combined effects of teachers' caring behavior and academic self-efficacy on the academic achievement of Chinese undergraduates: a fsQCA approach.
citation: Tang Chaoyong, Shi Yongzhi, Jiang Fan, Chen Wanming. (2026). The combined effects of teachers’ caring behavior and academic self-efficacy on the academic achievement of Chinese undergraduates: a fsQCA approach. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05227-5
title: fsQCA configurational method for studying academic achievement antecedents
description: The study employs fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, a set-theoretic method that "identifies multiple pathways leading to the same outcome, thereby enabling the analysis of multiple concurrent causalities." Five antecedent conditions were calibrated via indirect calibration using 95%, 50%, and 5% percentile anchors, with sufficiency thresholds set at consistency 0.800, frequency cutoff 3, and PRI consistency 0.750. Robustness tests raising the consistency threshold to 0.85, PRI to 0.78, and the frequency threshold to 4 left the configurations unchanged, confirming the findings' robustness.
requirements: Data calibration of all conditions and the outcome before necessity and sufficiency analysis
constraints: Applied to a cross-sectional self-report survey of 276 undergraduates at one Chinese agricultural university
target_learning_goals: Understanding configurational drivers of academic achievement
examples: The analysis used fsQCA 3.0 software and yielded complex, intermediate, and parsimonious solutions, with core conditions identified as those appearing in both parsimonious and intermediate solutions.
key_sources: Tang Chaoyong, Shi Yongzhi, Jiang Fan, Chen Wanming. (2026). The combined effects of teachers’ caring behavior and academic self-efficacy on the academic achievement of Chinese undergraduates: a fsQCA approach. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05227-5

article_title: Family-school-hospital collaboration model for urinary system tumor early screening education.
citation: Zhou Fen, Yu Ping, Yu Xiaofen, Han Xuyan, Wang Zheng. (2026). Family-school-hospital collaboration model for urinary system tumor early screening education. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1837667
title: 3D printing-assisted family-school-hospital collaborative education model for urinary system tumor early screening
description: An educational model combining 3D printing-assisted visual models of urinary system anatomy and pathology with a family-school-hospital collaborative program delivered via family WeChat groups over 6 months. Weekly online group activities included health education, case discussion and remote tutor guidance. The model integrates "3D visual training, multi-stakeholder collaboration, and family-level health decision-making" to cultivate medical interns' core competencies in tumor early detection.
requirements: Family WeChat groups with universal coverage among extended families in China
3D printing technology and professional medical digital software for model reconstruction
Clinical tutors, technical staff and family participants for multi-stakeholder collaboration
constraints: Validated only for urinary system tumors
Non-randomized convenience grouping by dormitory allocation
6-month intervention reflects only short-term effects
target_learning_goals: Urinary system tumor early screening knowledge
Core competencies including social medical curiosity, self-directed learning ability, doctor-patient communication, inter-professional teamwork, and transformative learning readiness
key_sources: Zhou Fen, Yu Ping, Yu Xiaofen, Han Xuyan, Wang Zheng. (2026). Family-school-hospital collaboration model for urinary system tumor early screening education. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1837667

article_title: Chiropractic students' characteristics influencing confidence and competence in modulating spinal manipulation force-time characteristics of specific target forces: a secondary analysis of a cross-sectional study.
citation: Nim C, Smith N, Starmer D, Wang S, Choi G, Alayed A, AlShareef J, Gnjatic A, Sloan K, Wong K, Funabashi M. (2025). Chiropractic students’ characteristics influencing confidence and competence in modulating spinal manipulation force–time characteristics of specific target forces: a secondary analysis of a cross-sectional study. Chiropractic & Manual Therapies. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12998-025-00577-0
title: Force-Sensing Table Technology (FSTT®) laboratory for teaching and assessing SMT force–time characteristics
description: The FSTT® is a force-sensing table used with a human analogue mannikin to teach and assess spinal manipulative therapy. The article states "The force-sensing devices provide students with quantifiable measures of their SMT performance by giving visual feedback on the biomechanical aspects of their SMT", including preload forces, peak forces and time to peak force, and that the devices reduce students' variability when delivering SMT. Outcomes were automatically analysed by standardized algorithms, and the FSTT® has demonstrated excellent reliability in measuring SMT force–time characteristics.
requirements: Access to the FSTT® laboratory; in this study students averaged 58 hours of lab attendance over the prior academic year
constraints: The article notes students are typically accustomed to real-time visual feedback during training, which is not readily available in real-world practice
target_learners: Chiropractic students learning spinal manipulative therapy
target_learning_goals: Accurate modulation of SMT preload, peak thrust force and time to peak force
examples: Students performed three practice thrusts then two posterior-to-anterior SMTs per target force (200 N, 400 N, 800 N) on a HAM® mannikin positioned on the FSTT®
key_sources: Nim C, Smith N, Starmer D, Wang S, Choi G, Alayed A, AlShareef J, Gnjatic A, Sloan K, Wong K, Funabashi M. (2025). Chiropractic students’ characteristics influencing confidence and competence in modulating spinal manipulation force–time characteristics of specific target forces: a secondary analysis of a cross-sectional study. Chiropractic & Manual Therapies. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12998-025-00577-0

article_title: Impact of a 3-year transformational change project in family violence clinical response: Qualitative evaluation of the depth and breadth of knowledge in hospital clinicians by training level.
citation: Troy K, Rushan C, Withiel TD, Felmingham KL, Fisher CA. (2025). Impact of a 3-year transformational change project in family violence clinical response: Qualitative evaluation of the depth and breadth of knowledge in hospital clinicians by training level. Women's Health, 21. https://doi.org/10.1177/17455057241305264
title: Family Safety Advocate clinical champions training programme with community of practice
description: The hospital's clinical champions pathway: 'The clinical champions programme provided in-depth training in evidence-based, best-practice responding when working with patients experiencing family violence (9+ hours in total)'. It combined staged training (a 3-h internal seminar plus 6.5-h external CRAF3 training in 2018-2019; from 2020 a 1-h self-paced online module and an 8-h live online seminar) with monthly clinical supervision and quarterly network meetings.
requirements: Further and ongoing resourcing, such as ongoing access to refresher training and a permanently funded family violence team that is available to support clinicians when needed
constraints: COVID-19 pandemic disruption in 2020 reduced the training provided and the number of attendees at training sessions relative to preceding years
target_learners: Hospital clinical staff, predominantly allied health professionals, with social workers the largest professional group
target_learning_goals: Risk assessment and management, safety planning, referrals, sensitive practice and responding to disclosures
examples: Between 2018 and 2019 training comprised a 3-h internal hospital seminar followed by 6.5-h external CRAF3 training; from 2020 the same content was delivered internally as a 1-h self-paced online module plus an 8-h live online seminar, with monthly drop-in supervision and quarterly network meetings thereafter

article_title: The association between students' confidence and ability to modulate spinal manipulation force-time characteristics of specific target forces: a cross-sectional study.
citation: Nim Casper et al. (2024). The association between students’ confidence and ability to modulate spinal manipulation force–time characteristics of specific target forces: a cross-sectional study. Chiropractic & Manual Therapies. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12998-024-00557-w
title: Force-sensing table technology (FSTT®) as a visual feedback training tool for SMT force–time modulation
description: The FSTT® is a modified treatment table with an embedded force plate that measures three-dimensional SMT forces at 2000 Hz and gives students immediate visual feedback on their force–time characteristics. The article describes it as "a training tool to quantify SMT forces and provide students with immediate feedback" and notes that twenty-one teaching institutions worldwide have integrated it into their curriculum. In this study it was used to record students' thrusts on a Human Analogue Manikin.
requirements: Requires students to practice without viewing the FSTT software window when performance is being assessed, since visible graphics and values would unblind the recordings
constraints: The force–time characteristics measured at the table interface have been found to differ from the applied forces, so they may not represent forces applied in clinical practice
target_learners: chiropractic students in first to third year of professional training
target_learning_goals: accurate modulation of SMT force–time characteristics (preload, peak impulse force, time to peak force)
examples: Participants performed posterior-to-anterior SMTs of 200N, 400N, and 800N on a prone Human Analogue Manikin while the FSTT recorded force–time characteristics at 2000 Hz.
key_sources: Nim Casper et al. (2024). The association between students’ confidence and ability to modulate spinal manipulation force–time characteristics of specific target forces: a cross-sectional study. Chiropractic & Manual Therapies. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12998-024-00557-w

article_title: Faculty standardized patients versus traditional teaching method to improve clinical competence among traditional Chinese medicine students: a prospective randomized controlled trial.
citation: Huang Meilan, Yang Han, Guo Jing, Fu Xiaoxu, Chen Wangshu, Li Bin, Zhou Shan, Xia Ting, Peng Sihan, Wen Lijuan, Ma Xiao, Zhang Yi, Zeng Jinhao. (2024). Faculty standardized patients versus traditional teaching method to improve clinical competence among traditional Chinese medicine students: a prospective randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05779-3
title: FSP-TCM six-step standardized patient simulation training model
description: The FSP-TCM model uses faculty members with at least 5 years of teaching experience, trained and certified as standardized patients for TCM, embedded in a 12-week, 36-credit-hour clinical skills course covering 12 representative TCM diseases. Its six-step process has the teacher lecture on each case's diseases, students discuss openly, the "SPs introduced students to information on the patient's personal data and disease conditions", the SP provides feedback on consultation and physical examination, students complete a medical history and treatment plan, and the teacher summarizes the case.
requirements: FSP volunteers need 5 or more years of teaching experience, health certification, confidentiality and informed consent agreements, and completion of a training program with three seasoned SP trainers followed by eligibility assessment
